payload: A musician muted the audio while pretending to play Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence' in an anechoic chamber -- literally producing no sound -- and YouTube's Content ID still hit the video with a copyright claim for the song. He stacks on two more absurd cases: a 5-second deliberately-mutated 'Smoke on the Water' riff that was claimed and whose dispute was rejected (risking a sponsored video getting deleted if he counter-disputes and loses), and a year-old joke short that was retroactively removed for 'harassment/cyberbullying,' putting a warning on his channel. His conclusion is that no video can be made copyright-proof -- even silence gets claimed, and the system carries zero risk for the trolls and all the risk for creators.
notes: Comedic rant/personal essay, not a how-to; the copyright-claimed 'song' is Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence', played as a silent-mute gag in a near-silent room.
Second grievance: a 5-second altered 'Smoke on the Water' riff claimed and dispute rejected; counter-disputing risks the whole (sponsored) video being deleted, so the sponsor could then sue him.
Third grievance: a ~1-year-old short (a mock baby-slap bit) taken down for cyberbullying/harassment, adding a channel warning; another warning becomes a strike.
Core argument: policies and automated systems change so old, once-fine videos can be flagged years later, with all risk shifted onto creators.
gaps: No claimant names, exact dollar amounts (the '$4' figure is a joke), or resolution outcomes are verified -- it is a one-sided creator account.
